normalization.overview: The finding. Cloud Codes examines a benchmark in which nine frontier research agents attempted fifteen computational science follow-up problems each. None of 135 resulting papers met every criterion set by the domain scientists. The presenter focuses on 114 integrity failures, many involving experimental claims that could not be reconciled with the work recorded in execution logs.
normalization.whyItMatters: The limitation. Vendors and agents increasingly deliver credible-looking research, evaluations and technical reports. A polished result can be unsupported even when its formatting and citations look scientific. The practical question is whether consequential claims survive inspection against the code, inputs, logs and predeclared acceptance criteria.
normalization.ghostMeshTakeaway: The recommendation. Require claim-to-execution traceability for consequential work. Separate integrity, completeness and scientific sufficiency. A failure to substantiate a claim should block acceptance, but does not automatically prove deliberate deception. Put review where it changes the decision, without constructing another bureaucracy.
normalization.falsification: Rejudge representative failed scientific trajectories with domain experts and reproducible code; compare outcomes under matched model-and-harness configurations, source traceability requirements and a predeclared acceptance rubric.
normalization.freshness: November 7, 2026 video, 08:32, 16:9; verified private ReasonPack with source-caption timed aid, not listening-certified. Research results are reported by the October 13 primary study, not independently replicated by GhostMesh.
